newsitem.title: TURKEY: SAfrica output fall to squeeze gold supply - analyst.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica output fall to squeeze gold supply - analyst.

text.p: Global gold supply will be squeezed sharply mainly because of an expected decline in the output of South Africa, the world's largest producer of the precious metal, a gold analyst said on Tuesday.

"How sharp that supply squeeze is depends to a large extent what happens in South Africa where some 60 tonne per year of capacity is slated to be taken out of production in the next five years," said Alan Mackie, gold specialist at the London- based Economic Intelligence Unit.
"Demand will have to slow down drastically or there will be a supply crunch which only the central banks could mitigate," he told a two-day International Gold Market conference in Istanbul.

He said the supply-demand imbalance could be shown since " ... the world's quoted mining companies can muster 18,700 tonnes of proven reserves at current prices, of which just under half should be available to the market."
Central banks might sell a "generous" 5,000 tonnes in the same period, bringing to 13,500 to 14,000 tonnes the available pool which also includes about 1,700 tonnes from forward sales, he said.
"This is barely enough to cover four years of current physical demand less recycled gold," he said.

He said another help to relieve the supply squeeze might come if South African ores, all facing intractible cost problems, could be brought into the play. If this occurred, "the 8,500-9,000 tonnes of available reserves would be doubled."
"But it would need a price of at least $500 per ounce to do this and the way costs are rising in many mines, closer to $600 per ounce by the year 2005" at 1995 prices, he said.

He said the physical gold demand in the five years was determined to a large extent by geographical factors, especially demand from the Souk, the informal wholesale-cum-retail markets of the Middle and Far East, where investment jewellery demand now accounts for 60 percent of the total physical demand.
"Chinese jewellery usage is going to be a key factor in future demand projection," he said, adding that China is fabricating around half the jewellery sold there.

"Although the modern gold market is still too immature to offer many clues as to the price levels at which the Souk will be a net seller of gold, there does seem to be a bottom of around $385 per ounce to the price at which level the Souk's absorptive power appears almost limitless," he said.
The Souk is estimated to hold about 26,000 tonnes in gold holdings.
